Property law is actually a very interesting area of law. But the questions you ask are hard to answer simply. The typical legal answer "it depends" applies in spades. Also, your two questions call upon different sets of rules because the first concerns personal property (a candy bar) and the second concerns real property (land). Real property has a whole host of special rules that are unique to real property.

Could I sell you a candy bar with an agreement saying only you will eat, and you can't sell it or give it to anyone else?

Yes, you can do something like that. You just need to structure the legal arrangement correctly. I note that you are talking about a candy bar, which is personal property. In any event, you wouldn't be selling the candy bar itself but the eating of it. If you sold the candy bar itself, then title would pass and the new owner could do what they want with it.

Could I sell you land under the condition that you don't allow any non-whites to enter it?

No. But that is for completely different reasons. One of the reasons courts will not honor otherwise valid legal arrangements is for purposes of public policy. Non-discrimination of the basis of race is one such policy. You could have done it a century ago. You could not do it today. Legal standards have changed.

Courts also will not respect provisions of wills which purport to do similar things. For instance, if you leave land to your daughter on the condition that she never sell to or allow any colored people to live on it, the court would respect the grant of the land, but not the restrictions.

For completely different reasons, you would have trouble telling her she couldn't sell it regardless of the buyer. That is because of a lot of rules which favor complete ownership and transferability of property. There are limits to how long you can entail property after you die. (See the movie Body Double for an example of one such principle called the Rule Against Perpetuities.)
